findings.title: Knowledge-family metrics are explicitly unavailable because the lesson and pack-hit ledgers are absent
findings.problem: §7.5's Knowledge family requires pack hit rate, citation rate, readiness blocks and lesson promotion rate computed from decision, inference_call and lesson rows, and §7.6 requires lesson promotion with >=2 independent evidence references and a person's review. The metrics source row is lesson, which the schema does not have: metrics.flow hard-codes knowledge.lesson_promotion_rate and knowledge.pack_hit_rate into the unavailable list, stating the lesson ledger (T8) is not in the schema and no knowledge-retrieval ledger exists. There is no lesson action module either (knowledge/ has only mod.rs and query.rs).

evidence.quote: reason: "the lesson ledger (T8) is not in the schema".to_owned(),
reason: "no knowledge-retrieval ledger exists; inference_call records the prompt, not the pack hit".to_owned(),

findings.failure_scenario: The Measure panel and the Knowledge family of the metrics API can never report a pack hit rate or a lesson promotion rate, so a tenant cannot tell whether retrieval is helping or whether lessons are being adopted. Because there is no lesson row, the >=2-independent-evidence promotion rule has no enforcement point: a single bad run cannot be promoted through a governed action because there is no action, and when one is added there is no ledger contract for it to check.
findings.acceptance: The lesson ledger (proposed/reviewed/promoted/rejected with evidence references) and a pack-hit source exist; metrics.flow reports real pack_hit_rate and lesson_promotion_rate; promotion refuses fewer than two distinct card/run/incident evidence references or a missing review; tests cover both refusals.

findings.title: A phase missing from the profile advances with zero mandatory artefacts
findings.problem: The gate reads only `profile.artifact_requirements`. When the requested phase has no entry (or an entry that is neither an array nor an object), the set list is empty and `satisfied` is initialised true, so the phase closes with no artefact at all; the `artifact_type.mandatory` column that carries the standard's own mandatory set is seeded and returned but never read by the gate. §8.1 says the mandatory set "comes from the standard, filtered by the tenant's adm_profile" — filtered, not replaced.
findings.failure_scenario: Adopt a profile that names requirements only for the phases walked so far (`artifact_requirements: {"preliminary": [...], "a": [...]}`, `contract_kinds: {}`) — the young-capability tailoring §8.1 encourages. Then `architecture.phases_advance {project_id: P, phase_code: "b"}`: sets is empty, satisfied is true, no contract kind is named, and the B node is written `accepted` with evidence `{"artifacts": [], "contract": null}`. Phases B–H can be walked producing nothing although the standard marks Business Service/Function, Data Entity Catalog, Technology Standards and the rest mandatory.
findings.acceptance: A phase with no explicit profile entry falls back to the standard's mandatory artifact_type set for that phase/plateau (or the profile is refused as un-tailored at adoption); advancing B with no approved Business Service/Function is refused by architecture_artifact_missing.

findings.title: Profile adoption accepts any UUID as its board decision
findings.problem: `adopt_profile_tx` writes the caller's `adopt_with_decision_id` into board_decision_id with no existence, gate, status or subject check, and `migrations/0054_architecture.sql` gives the column no foreign key to `approval` (contrast architecture_contract_approval_fk). The same codebase validates exactly this for contracts in `architecture.contracts_approve` (gate = architecture_board, status = approved, subject = this contract). §8.1's Preliminary gate is "the board adopts the profile"; here the gate is a client-supplied string.
findings.failure_scenario: Call `architecture.profile_tailor {key: "default", name: "Default", phase_set: [...], artifact_requirements: {...}, contract_kinds: {...}, adopt_with_decision_id: "<any random uuid>"}`. The profile returns 200 with status 'adopted' and no approval row exists anywhere in the tenant. The recorded capability baseline now claims board adoption, and every later phase gate runs against a profile whose adoption decision cannot be produced.
findings.acceptance: Adoption refuses unless the id names an approval row with gate='architecture_board', status='approved', subject_kind='adm_profile' and subject_id = this profile id; the migration carries the FK and a NOT NULL board_decision_id for status='adopted'.

findings.title: contracts_request retires another project's live contract via supersedes_id
findings.problem: `request_contract_tx` retires the row named by `supersedes_id` with an UPDATE scoped by tenant only — never by project, kind or phase — and then writes `superseded_by_id` on it unconditionally. Any contract id of the tenant is accepted, so a request for one project can retire the governing contract of another.

evidence.quote: WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status IN ('draft', 'live')",

findings.failure_scenario: Project P2 holds its live delivery_contract C2. A caller issues `architecture.contracts_request {project_id: P1, kind: "statement_of_architecture_work", phase_code: "a", title: "SAW", supersedes_id: C2}`. C2 flips to status='superseded' and its superseded_by_id now points at P1's SAW. P2's close gate then answers closure_contract_missing and `architecture.phases_advance` on G answers architecture_contract_not_live — two gates broken by a write to a different project.
findings.acceptance: A superseded contract must belong to the same project (and kind/phase) as the new one, else 409; a failed check writes neither the retirement nor the new row.

findings.title: phase_progress reports a phase evidenced by draft artefacts and superseded contracts
findings.problem: `phase_progress` builds `artifact_phases` from every architecture_artifact row the snapshot carries without testing `status`, and picks one contract per (project, phase) by recency without testing `status`; "evidenced" is then computed from those sets. The console therefore reports progress under a rule that contradicts `advance_phase_tx`, which only accepts an `approved` artefact and a `live` contract.
findings.failure_scenario: Create one artefact with `phase_code: "c"` and leave it in `draft` (or supersede an approved one), then read the snapshot: the project's phase_progress marks C `state: "evidenced"` and `next_required` moves to D, while `architecture.phases_advance {phase_code: "c"}` returns 409 architecture_artifact_missing. The Architecture destination and the gate disagree about the same phase.
findings.acceptance: phase_progress counts only status='approved' artefacts and status='live' contracts (matching advance_phase_tx), so a phase reported `evidenced` is one the gate would also close.

findings.title: Project start passes when the programme has no tranche row
findings.problem: assert_project_tranche_authorised_tx treats 'no tranche row found' as authorised. project_tranche_state_tx defaults a missing meta.tranche to 1 and returns None when no programme_tranche row has that number; the caller maps None to Ok(()). That None case is meant for standalone projects (programme_id NULL), but it is identical for a programme-bound project whose programme has no tranche rows at all, so the 'no project starts before the first tranche is authorised' rule is not enforced for a fresh programme.
findings.failure_scenario: A programme is created with programmes.create; nobody has created tranche 1 yet. A delivery project is created with programme_id set and meta.tranche=1. projects.create calls assert_project_tranche_authorised_tx, the tranche lookup returns no row, and the gate returns Ok. The project starts work, spends budget and produces outputs before any sponsoring-group tranche review, so the first-tranche authorisation requirement is skipped entirely.
findings.acceptance: For a project whose programme_id is set, a missing tranche row returns 409 tranche_not_authorised (only programme_id NULL may pass); an integration test creates a programme with zero tranches and asserts project start is refused.

findings.title: A benefit is accepted with no capability and no operational area
findings.problem: The spec's rule 'Every benefit names the capability it depends on and the operational area that must change' is not enforced. benefits.create defaults capabilities to an empty array and operational_area to the empty string, and the store validation (benefit_profile_missing over BenefitProfileFields) covers only baseline, target, measurement_method and benefit_owner_job_id. Neither capabilities nor operational_area is part of the validated field set on insert or update.
findings.failure_scenario: The BCM registers 'faster onboarding' with a baseline, target, method and owner but leaves capabilities and operational_area empty. benefits.create succeeds (only the four measurement fields are checked). The benefit enters the map with no capability dependency and no operational area to change, and can later be marked realized without any programme capability having been delivered or any part of operations having changed — the exact 'wish' the spec says must be refused.
findings.acceptance: benefits.create and benefits.update refuse 400 benefit_profile_incomplete unless capabilities is a non-empty array and operational_area is non-blank after trim, in addition to the four measurement fields.

findings.title: Benefits-map output_ref is free text, so dependency slips miss benefits
findings.problem: benefit_link.output_ref is a plain text column with no foreign key, and benefits.link copies the caller's string unchanged. The store's own contract for record_dependency_slip_tx says the at-risk benefits come from edges where benefit_link.output_ref names a wbs_node id, but no action validates that the string is an existing wbs_node of the programme. The map is therefore accepted with edges that can never participate in a dependency slip.

evidence.quote: /// The benefits come from the map's edges — `benefit_link.output_ref` names a `wbs_node` id —

findings.failure_scenario: The BCM links the benefit to output_ref '3.2.1 Onboarding walkthrough' (a WBS label) instead of the wbs_node UUID. benefits.link accepts it and the map is accepted. When that output's dependency slips, record_dependency_slip_tx matches benefit_link.output_ref against wbs_node ids, finds nothing, and reports zero benefits at risk; the benefit-at-risk metric and the sponsor's escalation both under-report by exactly the benefits the map intended to protect.
findings.acceptance: benefits.link resolves output_ref to an existing wbs_node id in the same programme (refusing a non-uuid or a node from another programme), or the dependency-slip path returns an error when an edge names no node instead of silently returning an empty list.

findings.title: Demo and retro cadence rows enforce nothing: no evidence, no credit, no lessons
findings.problem: 'demo' and 'retro' are accepted enum values and nothing else. No action requires each completed deliverable to exhibit its evidence at a system demo, no acceptance path withholds credit for a deliverable that was never demoed, and no retro action produces lessons or kata candidates. The spec's 'no demo, no credit' and inspect-and-adapt records have no implementation.
findings.failure_scenario: A PI closes without a system demo. Every deliverable stays accepted because acceptance is a status PATCH (see v2-w2c-4); the retro row exists with empty meta and produces no lesson or kata candidate. The improvement loop the spec says is measured has no rows to measure.
findings.acceptance: A demo cadence refuses to credit/accept a completed deliverable without a typed evidence reference exhibited at that demo, and a retro action writes lessons plus kata candidates linked to the retro cadence row; tests cover the refused credit and the written lessons.

findings.title: Baseline change guard trusts a self-declared 'approved' status on a register row
findings.problem: `take_baseline_guarded` advances a baseline when the named change row has `status == "approved"`, but `registers.create` and `registers.update` write any status string straight to the row with no validation and no approval gate. Any `portfolio:write` caller can create a change already marked approved, or PATCH an open one, and then re-baseline. The store already has `change_is_approved_tx`, which correctly reads the approval gate, but the baseline guard does not use it.

evidence.quote: /// gate is approved. The approval is the second principal's decision, not the row's status.

findings.failure_scenario: A delivery lead with portfolio:write creates a change row with status 'approved', baseline_ref pointing at the current approved baseline and meta.impact = {}. They then call baselines.take with that change_id. The new baseline is created and cited as advanced by an 'approved' change that no approver ever saw, bypassing §8.4 change control and §8.3's re-baseline rule entirely.
findings.acceptance: The baseline guard resolves approval through the approval table (gate='change', status='approved', meta.change_id matches), not the row status; register create/update refuse status='approved' for change rows (approval is only a gate effect). A test that self-declares approved and re-baselines must be rejected.

findings.title: The trace chain stops at card/project: no run, step, artefact or evidence end
findings.problem: The trace-edge whitelist is governed_asset | card | project. The spec chain continues WBS deliverable → card → run → step → artefact/evidence → acceptance → closure; none of run, step, artefact or evidence is an addressable end, and there is no view action joining them. Gate evidence edges also fire only for evidence items whose kind is governed_asset, so typed run/artefact evidence never leaves an edge at all.
findings.failure_scenario: An auditor asks the governance screen which requirement a given run proves and where its evidence is. trace_links.list can only return requirement→card or requirement→project edges; the run, its steps and its artefacts are unreachable from the requirement, and evidence arrays naming a run are silently skipped by the gate effect. The one question §8.5 says the screen answers cannot be answered.
findings.acceptance: Trace ends include run, step, artefact and evidence (tenant-resolved), and a bounded governance view action returns requirement → cards → runs → steps/artefacts/evidence for a requirement or run; tests build the chain and read it back.

findings.title: Trace links are optional and not required at creation for architecture-governed work
findings.problem: `trace_links.create` is a standalone opt-in action. Work-package/card creation (`wbs.create` and the board path) never checks for a trace link to an approved requirement or architecture asset. The spec requires the link at creation time for architecture-governed work; here it can be added later or never.
findings.failure_scenario: A team starts architecture-governed work (project meta marks it governed), creates the work package and card, and runs it with no requirement/architecture edge. The work is ungoverned and no run can be attributed to an approved requirement; nothing refuses the creation and no report flags the orphan.
findings.acceptance: Creation of a work package/card for an architecture-governed project refuses with 409 unless it carries a trace link to an approved requirement or architecture asset, writing the edge in the same transaction; a test asserts the orphan is refused and the linked creation succeeds.

findings.title: The andon cord can be released by a machine: andon.release never checks that the actor is a person
findings.problem: SPEC §9.2 says the andon cord is released by a person only. andon_release goes straight from the handler context to store::andon::release_tx; it never consults ctx.actor_kind, even though the same crate already uses actor_kind to decide whether an actor is a user (incidents.rs:750). The action is kind="internal", and the invoke boundary's Authority::Internal lane permits any actor_kind that holds the scope (invoke.rs:776), so a scheduled ops job or a coding agent holding andon:write can release a cord a human pulled. The release event records only actor_id, with no principal kind a reader could use to tell a person from a machine.
findings.failure_scenario: At 02:10 a human pulls the cord after a runaway deploy. An automation job (or a coding agent granted andon:write to 'unblock' itself) calls andon.release at 02:12. runs.create stops returning 409 andon-engaged and the worker resumes claiming runs for the tenant, including the pipeline that caused the incident. No human decision exists anywhere in the record, and the released event gives no way to tell the releaser was not a person.
findings.acceptance: andon.release returns 403 unless ctx.actor_kind == "user"; a test asserts a machine principal holding andon:write is refused while a user succeeds, and the andon.released event carries the principal kind.

findings.title: An incident that needed no write can never be postmortemed or resolved, starving the improvement loop
findings.problem: ops.postmortem refuses unless mitigated_at is recorded, and ops.resolve refuses unless both mitigated_at and a postmortem are present. An incident that self-heals, is fixed by a person outside conveyor, or is opened from an alert that then cleared has no mitigation write to run; it therefore can never produce a postmortem, a kata candidate, or a resolution, though §9.2 defines a person-opened incident and a postmortem whose systemic finding should become a kata.

evidence.quote: "a postmortem follows a mitigation; none has been recorded",

findings.failure_scenario: A certificate-expiry alert fires. An operator renews the certificate with their own tooling; conveyor's only write verbs (restart, scale, rollback, flag_flip) are not the fix and running one would be a false record. The incident stays open forever: no postmortem can be written, so the systemic finding (no automated rotation) never becomes a kata, and the card contaminates every open-incidents view and every severity metric.
findings.acceptance: An incident may record mitigation as 'no action required' with a reason (no cluster write, no mitigated write recorded) and may then be postmortemed and resolved; a test asserts a zero-write incident reaches resolved with a postmortem and, when systemic, exactly one kata candidate.

findings.title: The live web shell still exposes only V1's nine destinations; six V2 destinations have no route
findings.problem: apps/web/src/app.rs calls itself the nine-destination shell and its route table plus Sidebar (app.rs:267-322) contain no route or nav entry for Organisation, Authoring, Portfolio, Programme, Plan or Operations; Procedures/Improve exist only as Build sub-screens and an Evals sub-screen. Any deep link to a documented V2 destination falls through to the literal 'No such page.' fallback (app.rs:138). The §10.5 screens therefore cannot be reached in the live product at all.

evidence.quote: //! The application root: one boot, then the nine-destination shell.

findings.failure_scenario: The owner or a tenant admin opens /organisation, /portfolio, /programme or /operations (or clicks the destination in a design pack) and the SPA renders 'No such page.'; job catalogue/release administration, tranche reviews, benefits, WBS/baselines and incident/postmortem work have no human surface, so those workflows are API-only in practice.
findings.acceptance: Each §10.5 destination has a live route and Sidebar entry (Organisation, Procedures, Authoring, Portfolio, Programme, Plan, Improve, Operations), each landing on a real screen; or an owner-approved scope cut records the deferral in SPEC_V2 §10.5.

findings.title: The declared authoring.* action family does not exist
findings.problem: SPEC §10.4 declares authoring.intake|draft|review|publish and authoring.assets. The actions crate declares no authoring module (the module inventory spans lib.rs:20-107), and the compile-time registry is exactly the inventory submissions (registry.rs:184); enumeration of all ~493 declared names contains no authoring.* action, and served-spec.lock.json contains none. documents.* is the V1 document lifecycle and does not provide an asset draft catalogue or intake queue.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent front end or UI calls authoring.intake to submit a document to the authoring queue, or authoring.publish to release a drafted asset: the registry returns no such action (404/unknown action), so the Authoring destination's intake, draft catalogue, review/publish and dependency-status flows have no HTTP or MCP surface and can only be faked through ad-hoc documents.* calls.
findings.acceptance: authoring.intake|draft|review|publish and authoring.assets are registered ActionSpecs with handlers, appear in served-spec.lock.json and the MCP manifest, and a registry test asserts the five names; or SPEC_V2 §10.4 is amended by owner decision naming the replacement family.

findings.title: The kata.* family is not an action family; kata exists only as an unregistered process key
findings.problem: SPEC §10.4 declares kata.open|observe|analyse|propose|measure|adopt|propagate|close. No kata.* ActionSpec is registered. The implementation uses the string as a process-catalogue key: coach.escalate starts a process run with process_key 'kata.open' (coach.rs:780) and ops.incident names the same const (incidents.rs:64). There is no action to list a kata, read its Six Gests state, measure or adopt it, so the Improve destination's kata queue has no action surface.
findings.failure_scenario: coach.escalate opens a kata process run, but no kata.observe/measure/adopt action exists: an MCP client or the Improve screen cannot query the kata queue, record an observation/measurement or adopt the improvement, and the only way to advance it is the generic process_runs.start with a process key that must already be seeded. The systemic-improvement loop is not a discoverable API.
findings.acceptance: Either the eight kata verbs are registered as ActionSpecs (list/read state included) or SPEC §10.4 replaces the family with the process-key design and documents how observe/measure/adopt are expressed; a registry or process-catalogue test covers the chosen contract.

findings.title: Four of the six declared analyse.* actions are missing
findings.problem: SPEC §10.4 and §10.4.1 declare analyse.site, analyse.app, analyse.video, analyse.brand, analyse.content and analyse.report as the evidence producers for gates. Only analyse.site (analysis/actions.rs:16) and analyse.video (analysis/video.rs:16) are registered; there is no analyse.app, analyse.brand, analyse.content or analyse.report in the registry, so four of the six measured subjects named by §10.4.1 cannot be analysed through the action surface.
findings.failure_scenario: A production or QC procedure carries a gate that names analyse.brand or analyse.content (the §10.4.1 example: scoring the subject of the project, not the system). The action does not exist, so the gate cannot produce its evidence row and the step fails at resolution; brand/content/application/report QC is impossible without out-of-band work, while §10.4.1 forbids building it inside metrics/evals.
findings.acceptance: analyse.app, analyse.brand, analyse.content and analyse.report are registered with schemas and handlers (or explicitly scoped out in SPEC §10.4 by owner decision), and a registry test asserts the final six-verb set.

resolved_by.evidence: registered analyse.app, analyse.brand, analyse.content and analyse.report as read-only ActionSpecs over conveyor-analysis; the six-name registry test passes (analyse.app, analyse.brand, analyse.content, analyse.report, analyse.site, analyse.video); cargo-guard test -p conveyor-actions --test registry: 1 passed

findings.title: No spend budget gate: 429 tool_budget_exceeded is unimplemented and tool_call.cost is never written
findings.problem: §11.3 step 2 requires the broker to check the spend budget and fail with `429 tool_budget_exceeded`; §11.4's spend row requires 'budget check + ledger'; §11.8/§11.9 require cost per call. The broker performs only the effect-ceiling comparison (no budget read, no 429 branch anywhere in crates/), and writes the ledger row with `cost: None` unconditionally, so the column exists but is never populated and per-job 'tool-budget usage' cannot be computed.

evidence.quote: | **spend** | LLM generation, w2v render, TTS, paid data source | budget check + ledger |

findings.failure_scenario: A run whose binding permits `spend` calls `image_gen.generate` in a loop (image_gen is a first-wave toolkit). No budget counter is consulted before any of the calls; the destination produces paid renders on every iteration; every ledger row carries cost NULL, so the tenant's spend cannot be attributed and the gate that should have stopped at the first over-budget call never fires.
findings.acceptance: A spend-class tool call when the job's budget is exhausted returns `429 tool_budget_exceeded` before any network call; a successful spend call writes a non-null `cost` on its single `tool_call` row; a test drives `tools.call` for a spend tool under a zero budget and asserts the destination was never reached.

resolved_by.evidence: tool_budget 14/14: a spend tool with no budget or an exhausted one is refused 429 tool_budget_exceeded with zero upstream calls; a_priced_call_records_its_derived_cost writes the derived tool_call.cost; an_over_budget_inference_call_refuses_the_next_spend_before_the_backend gates the direct model path

findings.title: Write-verify is unenforced: no checks[]/verdict at call time and no publication gate for a write tool without verification
findings.problem: §11.3 states the two rules are 'not negotiable in the conveyor's registry': a write tool returns read-back `checks[]` and a `verdict`, and a write with no verification path cannot be published. The `tool` table has no verification declaration, `toolkits.publish` copies effect and schema from the action spec and inserts unconditionally, and the broker classifies the outcome from the HTTP status alone — it never inspects a `verdict` or `checks[]`. A write tool can therefore be published and called with no verification, and a 200 whose effect did not happen is ledgered `ok`.

evidence.quote: **Writes verify themselves.** A write tool returns read-back `checks[]` and a `verdict`; a write with no verification

findings.failure_scenario: A `write` tool (for example `coding.jobs.create`) is published with no checks declaration. The destination answers 200 after a partial write — the branch was created but the commit was not. The broker ledgers `ok`, the run proceeds on the belief that the write verified itself, and the unverified write is indistinguishable in the ledger from a verified one.
findings.acceptance: `toolkits.publish` refuses a `write`/`destructive` tool whose action declares no verification path, naming the tool; a call whose result carries a failing `verdict` or `checks[]` is ledgered `check_failed` and returned to the caller distinctly from `ok`; a test publishes a write tool with no verification and asserts no `tool` row is created.

resolved_by.evidence: tool_platform 11/11; a 200 whose own verdict/checks fail is ledgered check_failed with error_class write_not_verified. The publish half was already on main (0072_tool_meta), proved by estate_toolkits::a_write_tool_without_its_contract_is_refused

findings.title: idempotency='required' is data the broker never reads; the caller's key is a blind passthrough
findings.problem: The tool version declares `idempotency` (`required | optional | forbidden`), but resolve does not select it, the broker requires no key for a `required` write, and `tools.call` is itself declared `idempotent: false` so the engine does not replay. The only use of the key is copying whatever the caller supplied into the target request. §11.3's 'Writes take an `idempotency_key`' and §11.6's refusal to publish a write effect without an idempotency declaration are unenforced at call time.

evidence.quote: path cannot be published. Writes take an `idempotency_key`. These two rules are borrowed from the proven

findings.failure_scenario: An executor retries a write step after a transport timeout and sends no Idempotency-Key. Nothing at the broker refuses the call for a tool whose `idempotency='required'`; both attempts reach the destination and two branches (or two PRs, two uploads) exist for one step.
findings.acceptance: A call to a tool whose `idempotency='required'` with no key returns `422 tool_input_invalid` before any network call; `tool.idempotency` is resolved into the broker and a caller-supplied key is forwarded unchanged; a test asserts the missing-key refusal and that no destination call was made.

findings.title: credential_alias is resolved but never injected; every binding calls with the target's process credential
findings.problem: Resolve selects `b.credential_alias` into `ResolvedTool`, but no code reads that field. The broker dispatches the target action as `Authority::Internal` with no sealed-secret lookup, so the credential actually used is whatever the target's process configuration carries — identical for every tenant and every binding. §11.3 step 4 ('The broker injects it') and §11.1's 'narrowed by ... credential alias' have no implementation; the alias column is an authoritative-looking setting with no effect.

evidence.quote: 4. **Resolve the credential** from the sealed secret store by alias. The broker injects it; the prompt never carries it

findings.failure_scenario: Two tenant bindings pin the same toolkit with different credential aliases. Both calls are dispatched internally under the single configured service token, so tenant B's calls execute with tenant A's rights; revoking or rotating B's alias changes nothing at the destination, and a binding that declares no credential still succeeds on the target's ambient credential.
findings.acceptance: A call resolves the binding's `credential_alias` through the sealed secret store and the destination receives that credential; a binding with no alias against a toolkit whose auth adapter is not `none` fails closed before the call; a test binding two aliases to one toolkit asserts the two destination credentials differ.

findings.title: Long operations are unbounded in the required way: tool timeout_secs ignored, no pending status and no resume_token
findings.problem: The tool version carries `timeout_secs`, but the broker never applies it; the only deadline is the static 300 s `timeout_ms` on `tools.call`. On expiry the broker maps every non-2xx/412/422 outcome to `backend_error` — there is no `pending` branch, no `resume_token` is minted anywhere in crates/, and there is no status tool to continue from one. §11.3's 'on timeout the tool returns `pending` with a `resume_token`' and 'a timeout never fails silently' are unimplemented.

evidence.quote: **Long operations are bounded.** Every poll has a fixed budget; on timeout the tool returns `pending` with a
timeout_secs   int NOT NULL DEFAULT 30 CHECK (timeout_secs BETWEEN 1 AND 300),

findings.failure_scenario: A video-compiler render exceeds the 300 s action deadline. The broker ledgers `backend_error` and returns a failure, while the durable compile job keeps running at the destination. The run has no `pending` result and no `resume_token`, so it cannot poll or continue — a slow-but-succeeding operation is recorded as a backend failure and the work is orphaned.
findings.acceptance: A call whose destination exceeds the tool's `timeout_secs` returns `{status:"pending", resume_token}` and ledgers status `pending`, not `backend_error`; the matching status tool accepts the token and continues; a test with a slow destination asserts the pending envelope and a follow-up call that completes.

findings.title: No BYO surface: the publishable catalogue is a compile-time seed and no OpenAPI import or MCP discovery action exists
findings.problem: §11.5 permits a tenant two kinds of tool: an OpenAPI 3.1 toolkit imported as a draft with tenant-admin approval and a contract test, and a remote MCP server with binding-scoped discovery. The only publish path is `toolkits.publish`, whose input is `EmptyIn` and whose source is the compile-time `RAW` list of `seed/toolkits/*.json`; `ToolkitManifest` carries no document, schema or URL, and the registered tool actions are only `tools.call`, `tools.usage`, `tools.probe` and `toolkits.publish`. There is no import action, no tenant allowlist and no discovery, so a tenant's own licensed service cannot enter the estate at all.

evidence.quote: A tenant may bring two kinds of tool and only two:
//! the broker dispatches. It never carries an input schema: the schema is copied from the live

findings.failure_scenario: A tenant licensed for its own internal OpenAPI service asks for it as a tool. There is no request an admin can make: publishing reads only the embedded seed files, the toolkit manifest cannot express the tenant's document or base URL, and no tenant allowlist exists to review the destination. The tenant's jobs cannot call their own service, and §11.3 step 5's BYO allowlist has nothing to attach to.
findings.acceptance: A tenant-admin action imports an OpenAPI 3.1 document into a draft toolkit (per-operation closed schemas, default `read` effect, destination base URL, credential alias) that cannot be bound until a contract test and approval pass; an MCP endpoint registers and exposes only the bound subset; no path accepts uploaded code. A test creates a tenant toolkit from a document and binds it to a run.

findings.title: Earned auto-merge is replaced by an unconditional policy waiver
findings.problem: §9.3/D34 require auto-merge to be an approval_policy row with `approver_kind='auto'` and typed conditions — consecutive green runs, revert count, path scope, independent reviewer, expiry — all tenant configuration, and the policy change itself a gated change. The implemented policy has exactly two fields, `approval` (required|waived) and `self_approval`, and `waives()` returns true for any action whose row says `waived`. There are no conditions, no expiry, no revert or reviewer inputs, no version dimension, and `approval_policies.set` is an ordinary `write` action, so the policy is not itself gated. A single holder of `approvals:write` can permanently switch a destructive gate off.

evidence.quote: /// This tenant has opted out for this action; the call runs without one.

findings.failure_scenario: A tenant sets `waived` for ops.rollback (or any destructive action). From then on every rollback runs without an approval, with no condition, expiry or revocation trigger, and the change that enabled it was itself ungated. R6's 'auto-merge earned and revocable' becomes a permanent off switch that no green-run or revert-count evidence can turn back on.
findings.acceptance: Autonomy is a versioned policy row carrying approver kind and typed conditions plus expiry; it defaults off, is revoked automatically when a condition fails, and a change to it requires an approval decision rather than a plain write.

findings.title: self_approval='allowed' lets a requester decide their own gate
findings.problem: P4 and §5.4 state flatly that the executor/assignee/requester cannot approve the gate that judges their work. The policy model adds a second opt-out, `self_approval` (forbidden|allowed), and the decision writer consults `allows_self_approval` for the gate's action. Setting `allowed` therefore makes the requester a valid approver for their own gate, so dual control and P4 are tenant-waivable configuration rather than invariants.
findings.failure_scenario: The only holder of `approvals:write` sets self_approval=allowed for ops.scale, then requests a scale gate and approves it themselves. The audit records one human decision by the requester and the gate resolves; no second person ever saw the action, and nothing flags the self-approval as an exception.
findings.acceptance: Self-approval is unconditional: the decision writer refuses a decision whose approver is the gate's requester/executor, with no policy row able to relax it. Any historical exception is an explicit, audited override rather than a stored permission.

findings.title: never_refused counts only reject decisions and ignores every other refusal
findings.problem: §5.4 defines the governance audit over gates that have 'never refused anything in a full programme cycle'. The implementation computes never_refused as decided approvals with zero rejected approvals, where `rejected` counts only approval rows whose status became rejected. Refusals that happen before or outside a decision — 422 gate_evidence_missing at request time, 403 approval_wrong_target/approval_not_approved at the invoke boundary, expired gates — create or change no rejected approval row and are invisible. The window also defaults to a rolling 90 days, not a programme cycle.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate refuses every evidence-less submission at request time (no approval row is written) and approves the few evidenced ones. Its governance row shows decided>0 and rejected=0, so it is reported as never refused, while a gate that genuinely never refused but had one rejection 91 days ago is reported healthy. The audit flags the wrong gates and misses the real rubber stamp.
findings.acceptance: Every refusal path (evidence 422, target/action 403, expiry) increments the gate's refusal count; the window is the programme cycle (or a configured equivalent), and the audit opens a finding/event rather than only populating a read-model field.

findings.title: metric_reconciliation is a write-only aggregate with a dead verdict helper
findings.problem: P10 forbids an aggregate with no named procedure and no metric reading it. `metric_reconciliation` rows are written by metrics.reconcile (both the matched/difference path and the unavailable path), but no action, metric or read model ever reads them; the only helper that consumes the verdict is parked behind `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a comment saying it waits for a later action. The billing comparison therefore exists only as the response of the call that recorded it, not as a governance figure.

evidence.quote: // Keep the reconciliation enum referenced until the P2 action lands on this branch; the state

findings.failure_scenario: A monthly reconciliation records a growing conveyor-vs-billing delta and opens an incident card each time. No report, dashboard or metric ever queries the reconciliation table, so the trend across periods is invisible; if the incident cards are closed, the delta history is buried in rows nothing reads. If the service is later removed, the table and writer remain as pure dead weight.
findings.acceptance: A declared read action/metric returns reconciliation history (latest state per period, delta trend, incident links), or the table, writer and dead helper are deleted until a consumer exists.

findings.title: T14 closed on source-code evidence although its gate demands live probe and live-call receipts
findings.problem: T14's gate requires, for each published toolkit, a probe and one live call, a scale-up/scale-back of scientific_processor, a zero-use report and an outage-unbind test. The project register closes T14 with a required 'closure-review' output, but coverage cites only the source directory crates/actions/src/toolkits — no probe result, call ledger, scale receipt or closure review is cited. A code path cannot prove a live estate call.
findings.failure_scenario: A toolkit is published and bound from unit code alone; its backend is unreachable or its schema drifted. Jobs bind an unprobed tool, calls fail mid-run, and the zero-use/outage behaviour was never exercised. The estate coverage claim is false until a live call is recorded.
findings.acceptance: T14 reopens unless the closure evidence carries: one live probe + live call receipt per published toolkit; the scientific_processor scale-up/scale-back log; a zero-use report; and a recorded outage-unbind test. Every receipt is addressable from the public output index.

findings.title: T8 marked built on source and migration evidence with no cited behaviour test
findings.problem: The organisational-memory gate is behavioural: a lesson with one evidence ref must be refused, and two independent refs plus review must promote a source draft. findings.title: T3 closed with the specification itself as its only evidence

findings.title: Partial mandatory artefacts are suppressed by COVERED_BY, contradicting the declared absent-only contract
findings.problem: coverage_key() is consulted for every non-evidenced mandatory artefact, including partial ones. The file's own contract says a partial artefact must NOT be covered because a published document missing a required heading is a section-level finding the data-gap rules cannot see. Because the lookup ignores status, a partial phase/project artefact is attributed to the generic gap package, no finding is emitted, and no package ever names the missing heading.

evidence.quote: # but the package is the gap rule's: one defect, one package. A partial artefact is NOT covered,

findings.failure_scenario: A mandatory phase-B artefact for T9 is partial: its published document lacks the required 'Business Interaction' heading while other sections resolved, and the gap mandatory_artefacts:T9 exists. build_findings calls coverage_key, matches COVERED_BY['phase-b'], emits no finding, and the published register carries only the generic gap whose Definition of Done is 'the next audit reports no gap', not 'the heading is written'. The artefact can then flip to evidenced through unrelated doc presence, and the public rail never showed the section-level defect.
findings.acceptance: coverage_key returns "" unless artefact["status"] == "absent" (absent-only for both maps), and a self-test case proves: partial phase artefact + matching gap => exactly one section-level finding and no suppression.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #530 before merge

findings.title: A published document with no rendered page satisfies every required section
findings.problem: document_headings() returns None when output-<id>.html is absent, and resolve_documents counts a None-heading document as matched for ANY heading. The section then carries count > 0, reads evidenced, and heading_found is True, so no partial/absent status and no finding is produced even though no page exists to contain the heading. The section-level honesty check is silently disabled by a missing artefact.

evidence.quote: if headings[str(doc.get("id"))] is None or heading_key in headings[str(doc.get("id"))]
return source, bool(matched) or not docs

findings.failure_scenario: artefacts.json publishes document d7 for project T5 (published_at set), but the snapshot emits no output-d7.html into --outputs-dir. Every section of T5's document-backed artefact matches d7, the artefact is classified evidenced, no finding is emitted, and check-standards hashes only the generated standards page, so the record publishes green while its cited source has no page to open.
findings.acceptance: A None heading set means unverifiable, not matched: count only documents whose headings were actually read, and a self-test with a published doc row whose page is absent expects partial or absent plus a finding.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #530 before merge

findings.title: The architecture capability computed source emits a phantom profile row when no profile exists
findings.problem: computed_rows('architecture_capability') indexes the profile list with `or [{}]`, so the returned rows always contain at least {kind: 'profile'} even when the snapshot has no adm_profile. Any required section whose source is this computed name reports count 1 and reads evidenced, asserting a capability the row set does not support.
findings.failure_scenario: The tenant has not established the Preliminary capability: architecture.profiles is empty (the state v2.js itself renders as 'no profile yet'). The capability artefact's profile-backed required sections receive the phantom profile row, count 1, and the artefacts that depend on this source are published as evidenced with no profile, no board and no maturity rows behind them.
findings.acceptance: Return [] when profiles is empty (drop the `or [{}]` fallback) and add a self-test asserting the capability artefact is absent on a profile-less fixture.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #530 before merge

findings.title: check-standards recomputes status from self-reported section statuses and never verifies sources or the live register
findings.problem: The gate derives an artefact's expected status from section.status strings rather than from section source counts, and accepts package_published as an authoritative boolean without reading the published rework register. A record can therefore claim evidenced sections with zero-count sources and a package that no card exists for, and still pass.
findings.failure_scenario: A hand-edited or partially regenerated standards.json marks a section evidenced with every source count 0 and sets package_published true while naming a package key absent from data/rework.json. check-standards exits 0, the homepage's make verify ships the false record, and the view rail points a reader at a rework card nobody opened.
findings.acceptance: Recompute each section's status from its sources (evidenced only when some source count > 0) and resolve package_key against the packages array in data/rework.json; add self-test cases for both forgeries.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #530 before merge

findings.title: publish-data.sh writes into the published pack before the conformance gate
findings.problem: Step 0 runs build-docs.py against $pack/docs before the snapshot, the audit and the strict gate. A failed publish therefore still leaves the pack's rendered pages rewritten, directly contradicting the script's stated contract that a failed audit leaves the published data and output pages untouched.

evidence.quote: # A failed audit therefore leaves the published data and output pages untouched.

findings.failure_scenario: The strict gate exits non-zero on a P0 at line 107; by then step 0 has already regenerated docs pages in the working pack. The operator is told the publish left things untouched but the tree is dirty, and a later publish or a manual rsync carries the half-updated pages with no gate having approved them.
findings.acceptance: Build rendered pages into $tmp/docs and copy them in at step 4 with the rest of the pack (or restore the pack on any exit), plus a test that a forced strict failure leaves the pack byte-identical.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #530 before merge

findings.title: A pinned release does not pin the executor configuration that runs
findings.problem: Execution reads model_ref, prompt_ref, allowed_actions and the iteration and timeout limits from the live capability_agents row, never from the binding's release_snapshot, so the release hash does not describe the configuration that ran.

evidence.quote: let record = store::capability::get_agent_tx(&mut tx, tenant, agent_id)

findings.failure_scenario: Publish release R and bind it; run once with model medium and grants G1. Call capability_agents.update to router/large with G2. The next run executes the new model and grants under the unchanged release hash R, and neither the run nor the ledger records the change.
findings.acceptance: Execution resolves model_ref, prompt_ref, allowed_actions and the limits from binding.release_snapshot (or pins an immutable agent version); editing an agent used by an active binding requires a new release and binding; a test mutates the agent and asserts the pinned run still uses the snapshot.

resolved_by.evidence: agent.rs resolves max_iterations and timeout_ms from the release anatomy (effective_max_iterations/effective_timeout_ms) when a release is present; the runtime test seeds a live agent (router/medium) different from the release pin (router/release) and compiles the request with the binding's release anatomy, not the live row

findings.title: An internal_agent binding's pinned agent is never the agent that runs
findings.problem: The binding stores capability_agent_id, but a process run resolves its executor from the process's bound agents or the capability's active agents, so the recorded executor and the executed one can differ with no refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: Create an internal_agent binding that pins agent A. Start a run of a process whose step names agent B, or whose capability has one active agent B. The run executes B and records A's binding and release hash; nothing refuses or flags the divergence, and readiness checks the process's agents rather than the binding's.
findings.acceptance: Execution resolves the capability agent through the run's job binding, or refuses a step agent that differs from the binding with a 409; a test pins A and resolves B and asserts the refusal, and every run's recorded agent equals its binding's.

findings.title: A new binding goes live with no decision

findings.acceptance: Creating or activating a binding opens a gated decision; only an approved decision flips it to active, and a direct status=active request is refused until then; tests cover the refusal and the approval.

findings.resolved_by: fixed in #612 before merge; the Memory source renders the run's prior steps, the card's hot rows and one digest, and a required memory source with nothing to select still refuses by name (crates/domain/tests/prompt_memory.rs, crates/store/tests/prompt_catalogue.rs)

findings.title: job_catalogue.list has no search or pagination

findings.title: project_register_item.links does not implement the declared shape
findings.problem: §5.5 declares links as {cards[], requirements[], decisions[]}; the column defaults to an array, create defaults to an empty array, and the only internal writer appends {kind,id} entries.

findings.title: The SOP source review gate is hard-coded to a human
findings.problem: §5.6 says every SOP-derived artefact sits behind a review gate whose default is human and is tenant-configurable; procedures.review_source refuses every non-user actor and reads no tenant policy.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant configures source review to a rule or dual-control gate; the setting is ignored, every non-human review is refused with a 403, and an automated pre-review or a non-human second decider cannot be used.
findings.acceptance: The review gate kind resolves from tenant configuration with human as the default; a test shows a configured rule decider is accepted and an unconfigured agent is refused.

findings.title: SOP intake has no batch path
findings.problem: §5.6 says a tenant supplies SOPs singly or as a batch and that a batch never publishes itself; every intake action takes one source.
findings.failure_scenario: Onboarding 200 SOPs forces 200 calls; a mid-run failure leaves a partially ingested set with no batch record, and the guarantee that a batch never publishes itself has no batch to enforce.
findings.acceptance: Intake accepts an array of sources, or a batch action, producing N unpublished drafts with per-item results; a two-source test publishes nothing.

findings.title: The authoring pipeline is an inline converter call, not a procedure job
findings.problem: §5.7 requires the authoring family to be ordinary jobs on the two executors and the pipeline to be a procedure; procedures.ingest_sop calls the converter inside the action and records no job or run.
findings.failure_scenario: A long SOP exceeds the action timeout; the conversion fails before the source asset is written, nothing durable can be retried, no executor isolates the call, and no authoring run is measured.
findings.acceptance: Conversion runs as a job driven by a published procedure with a run row per intake and a retry; a test proves a converter failure leaves the source recorded and retryable.

findings.title: No dev.* action family exists for the nine-step development gate set
findings.problem: §9.1 defines charter, lane branch, implement, verify, review, merge gate, deploy with live verification and close as gated steps; the action registry enumerates every registered action and none is a dev.* action, so the cycle has no execution surface. v1-p6-2 records the missing trigger in the improvement loop; this records the missing pipeline itself.

evidence.quote: `development` type and a stricter gate set:

findings.failure_scenario: T6's lane, PR, CI, review, merge, deploy and live verify is attempted on conveyor itself; there is no action to open the lane, record verification, request the review or record the deploy, so the only record is prose and no gate can refuse a red merge.
findings.acceptance: dev.open, dev.implement, dev.verify, dev.review, dev.merge, dev.release and dev.rollback are registered ActionSpecs, or a seeded process map bound to the development type, each writing its evidence row; a test refuses a merge with red verification and a release without a rollback plan.

findings.title: A completed eval run pins no instrument digest
findings.problem: §9.3 freezes eval versions per measurement; eval_cases.update rewrites a case in place with no version or status guard, and eval_run stores only version_id, so a completed measurement cannot be reproduced after an edit.

evidence.quote: creates a new version and voids its sign-offs.

findings.failure_scenario: A candidate is measured on version 3 and adopted; later eval_cases.update rewrites a case in version 3. Readiness voids the sign-offs, but the completed run and its report still point at version 3, so before and after scores are no longer reproducible or distinguishable.
findings.acceptance: eval_run stores the instrument digest it measured, or edits mint a new version; a test edits a case cited by a completed run and asserts either that the edit is refused or that the run's digest still identifies the measured instrument.

findings.title: No deploy or live-verify gate; ops.rollback is a kubectl undo
findings.problem: §9.1 requires rollout by image digest, a /health check, the slice's acceptance check and a rollback plan before deploy, and §9.3 refuses a deploy without a tested rollback; the registry has no deploy or release action for a project and the only rollback restores a pod template revision.

evidence.quote: /// `ops.rollback` — restore the pod template of an earlier revision (`kubectl rollout undo`).
- **Rollback is mandatory** for deployable changes; a deploy without a tested rollback is refused.

findings.failure_scenario: A change merges and a person deploys it by hand; no image digest, /health result or acceptance row is written, and a later ops.rollback only undoes a ReplicaSet revision citing no rollback plan. The rule that a deploy without a tested rollback is refused has no refusal point.
findings.acceptance: A dev release action records the image digest, the /health result, the slice acceptance evidence and a rollback-plan reference, refusing a missing or failed rollback plan and a missing live check; tests assert each refusal and that release is a separate decision from merge.

findings.title: A handoff is not expressible: no cards.assign and no binding on a card
findings.problem: §6.6 requires a handoff card to name its job binding, inputs and acceptance and to be produced by cards.assign or cards.move with a comment; card.job_binding_id exists in the schema but no code writes or reads it and cards.assign does not exist.

evidence.quote: 2. **A handoff is an action** (`cards.assign` / `cards.move` + `comment`/`artifact.attach`) producing an `event`.

findings.failure_scenario: The PM needs delivery binding J-4 to do WP-3 and calls cards.create. The row lands with job_binding_id NULL and no acceptance, and any delivery binding with cards:write can claim it; the run starts with no binding, so which job was asked, and what done means, is unrecorded and unauditable.
findings.acceptance: A handoff action (cards.assign, or a binding on create) requires an active job_binding_id plus artefact ids and acceptance criteria, writes card.job_binding_id, emits an event and is exposed on CardOut; moving a delivery card into a work lane without a binding is refused 422; a test proves the binding reaches the run.

findings.title: pm.plan replaces an approved baseline without a change request

This is the baseline path: v1-p5-4 is the WBS row mutation path and they share one missing guard.

evidence.quote: "project {project_id} already holds an approved {kind} baseline ({}); a new \
| **Never** | approve its own gates; change an approved baseline without a change request; do the work of a delivery job |

The PM runs pm.plan again with added nodes: a second scope baseline is inserted with change_id NULL, its gate opens and is approved, and the latest approved baseline is the changed scope. No change register row exists.
findings.acceptance: plan_project refuses with 409 change_request_required when an approved baseline of that kind exists unless an approved change naming it is supplied, and refuses the duplicate WBS; a test re-calls pm.plan and projects.baseline after approval and asserts the refusal, and both paths share one guard.

findings.title: The PM's status report output has no producer
findings.problem: §6.1 lists a status report and an LLM status narrative as PM outputs; no action, asset kind or console surface produces one, and pm.get is a raw read of the project, charter, WBS, baselines and gates.

findings.failure_scenario: A sponsor asks for the project's status. The PM can only dump rows through pm.get; no report asset exists to gate, version or cite at a tranche review, so status reporting happens outside the governed record and cannot be audited.
findings.acceptance: A pm.status action writes or returns a report with the PM's status narrative scoped to the project, WBS and gates, backed by a status-report asset kind or a documented non-asset contract; a test asserts the report cites the live baseline and gate set.

findings.title: A missing operation dead-ends instead of opening a tool request
findings.problem: §11.6 makes a missing operation a governed path: the procedure step opens a tool-request card, a development job implements and publishes it, and the step is rebound; intake instead refuses the whole source with 422 sop.cannot_grant_tool, and no tool-request action or card type exists.

findings.failure_scenario: An author ingests a procedure whose step needs an operation no tool provides. The intake is refused with no record of what was missing, and no card is opened; the procedure can never acquire the tool, so it stays permanently invalid and the gap is invisible to the tool estate.
findings.acceptance: A missing operation creates a tool-request card naming the operation, the step and the procedure; publishing a tool version rebinds the step; a test ingests such a procedure, asserts the card exists and that the procedure is retryable once the tool is published.

findings.title: Zero-use tools are flagged but never retired, and a schema drift opens no kata
findings.problem: §11.9 requires a zero-call tool to be retired over a cycle and a schema-drift signature to open a kata; tools.usage computes zero_use and nothing consumes it, there is no tools.retire action, and a backend 422 is ledgered as check_failed.

A backend changes under its contract; every call is ledgered check_failed and no kata is opened, so the drift is a silent per-call failure.
findings.acceptance: tools.retire unbinds and retires a zero-use tool with an owner decision, and a schema-drift signature opens a kata; a test drives a zero-use window to retirement and a 422 drift to a kata row.

findings.title: Job object storage has no live path: JobStorage is test-only
findings.problem: §11.10 requires one storage adapter that writes and reads MinIO directly with a tenant prefix, encryption, a content hash and a size cap; JobStorage implements that contract but no registered action, broker tool or toolkit calls it, so a run cannot persist bytes.

findings.failure_scenario: A run produces bytes and has no way to persist them: no action exposes JobStorage, so the tenant prefix, SSE, hash and size cap never execute inside a job. The storage cap of the tool contract is satisfiable only by tests calling the adapter directly.
findings.acceptance: A storage action or broker tool exposes get and put through JobStorage with the tenant prefix, SSE, hash and cap enforced at the call path; a test stores and retrieves a job's object through the action and refuses a cross-tenant key and an oversize object.

findings.title: A run can call a model with no compiled prompt and a NULL prompt hash
findings.problem: §7.7 requires every prompt to be compiled at run time from the run's sources with a recorded hash; agent.run compiles only when prompt_ref is Some, readiness skips the check when it is None, and the domain claims a default that does not exist.

evidence.quote: /// A built-in `<name>@<version>`, or `None` to use the action's default.

findings.failure_scenario: capability_agents.create with prompt_ref null and status active succeeds; a process run resolves it, readiness passes, agent.run sends the step-input messages and the model answers; inference_call records a NULL prompt hash, so the call is not reproducible and can carry an arbitrary caller-supplied system message.
findings.acceptance: Creating or activating an internal_agent without a resolvable prompt_ref is refused, readiness blocks it and agent.run cannot call a model without compiled text; a test proves a NULL prompt_ref yields zero calls and every internal_agent call carries a 64-hex prompt hash.
findings.resolved_by: fixed in #697 before merge: an active internal_agent must name a resolvable prompt (domain validate_agent_config, create/update 422 prompt_ref_required, readiness prompt_not_configured, and agent.run refuses 409 before any inference), and every recorded call carries a 64-hex prompt_sha256 (crates/actions/tests/capability.rs, agent_run_resolved.rs, internal_agent_runtime.rs)

findings.title: Workflow and generic runs bypass the required-knowledge readiness guard
findings.problem: The only readiness call is in process_runs.start; workflow_runs.start and runs.create insert runs with capability_id None, so §7.6's required-pack block never runs there and the compile receives no capability or knowledge facts.

The required pack is never enforced before the first step.
findings.acceptance: Every run-start seam either resolves capability_id, including workflow and generic runs, or runs the same readiness check; a test starts a workflow run against a required unpublished pack and asserts the refusal with zero run rows and zero model calls.

findings.title: Prompt character budgets cannot be written, so the over-budget refusal is unreachable
findings.problem: §7.7 requires compiled prompts with character budgets and a measured refusal over budget; both seed inserts omit budget_chars and no action writes the column, so every recipe stays unbounded.

findings.acceptance: An action can set and version prompt.budget_chars and prompt_section.budget_chars; with a tight ceiling the compile refuses with the measured size over the limit and makes no model call; a test sets a ceiling and asserts the refusal.

fixed in #612 before merge; hot_for_card_tx excludes digest rows, so memory.recall's hot is the record and the digest is reachable only through the prompt selector's include_digest and the cold read (crates/store/tests/memory.rs)
findings.title: memory.recall serves the consolidated digest inside the hot rows
findings.problem: §7.6 separates hot rows from the cold digest; consolidation writes the digest into work_package_memory as kind digest and the hot query has no kind filter, so recall returns a derived digest body as a hot row.

evidence.quote: /// One memory row as an action returns it. Never carries a digest body: that is read from strata.

findings.failure_scenario: After a run completes and memory.consolidate writes a digest, memory.recall for that card returns a hot entry of kind digest carrying the full, possibly stale, digest text beside the real hot rows and the cold hits. A consumer that reads hot as the record acts on a derived fact that a newer hot row has already superseded.

findings.title: A per-step judge verdict is a second decision store
findings.problem: §10.1 requires one record per fact; the step judge's accept or reject is persisted only as JSON on run_step.judge, with no decision row, so the per-step choice lives in a store the model does not declare.
findings.failure_scenario: A laya judge rejects a step. ladder.list returns nothing for that gate, and the row carries no policy version, input hash or latency, so the refusal is unreproducible and invisible to the reporting that finds gates which never refuse.
findings.acceptance: Every laya, checker and eval verdict writes one decision row with rung, answer, versions, input hash and latency, linked to the run step in the same transaction; a test asserts the decision count equals the judged steps and that ladder.list returns the step gate.

findings.title: laya's 3 second hard budget is enforced as 60 seconds
findings.problem: §10.2 fixes the conveyor-to-laya seam at a 1500 ms default with a 3 s hard budget; the only laya action declares a 60 s timeout and the invoker enforces that value, so no 1500 or 3000 ms constant exists.

evidence.quote: | conveyor → laya | `POST /v1/systemone`, 1500 ms default / 3 s hard budget; fail policy per decision policy |

findings.failure_scenario: The laya bridge accepts connections and stops answering; every judge call holds a worker for 30 seconds, and the decision policy's unavailable path cannot run inside the contract, so a stalled laya becomes a worker starvation event.
